To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the enzymes in the pathway for the catabolism of (D)-gluconate and (D)-galactarate in Escherichiacoli are encoded by three transcriptional units.

we have characterized the enzymes and the genes encoding the enzymes involved in the catabolism of the hexaric acids (D)-gluacrate and galactarate, and have identified a gene encoding an enzyme that is related to the GlucD enzyme but which is significantly impaired in its ability to catalyze the dehydration and epimerization of the hexarate substrates.

we have identified the genes encoding the enzymes of a novel pathway for the metabolism of (D)-gluconate, (D)-galactonate, (D,L)-glucaric acid, (D,L,L)-galactaric acid, and (D,L,L,L)-tartronic acid, and we have characterized the enzymatic activities of these enzymes.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification and characterization of the (L)-idaric acid catabolic pathway and its evolutionary relationship to the (D)-galactarate catarbolic pathway in E. coli and the (D)-arabonate catabolic pathways in Pseudomonas sp. and Rhizobium sp.
the evolution of the enolase (2-phospho-D-glycerate hydratase) superfamily.
the identification and characterization of genes encoding the enzymes involved in the catabolic pathways of (L)-idaric acid and the (D)- and (L)-glucaric acid/galactaric acid isomers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the (D)- and (L)-glucaric acid dehydratases of the E. coli K-12 genome have evolved to be more specific to (D)-gluconate and (L-)idarate, respectively, whereas the GlucDRP of E. coli K12 has not yet evolved to become more specific to either (D)- or (L)-gluconic acid.
the genes encoding the enzymes involved in the catabolism of (D)-gluconate, 5-ketogluconate, and glucarate are present in the E. coli genome.
GlucD, galactarate/GlucDRP, and the aldolase are the first examples of the evolution of the enolase fold to catalyze the dehydratases and aldolases of a new class of sugars.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have characterized the (D)-galactarate/(D)-glucaro-1,4-lactone catabolic pathway of E. coli and that this pathway has evolved by the recruitment and/or evolution of the enolase and phosphoglycerate mutase superfamily members.

the (D)-galactarate/(D)-glucuronate catabolic pathways in E. coli are similar in many respects to the (L)-tartrate/(L)-gluconate catabolic system, and the enzymes in both pathways are members of the enolase (or phosphopyruvate hydratase) superfamily.
E. coli has a (D)-gluconic acid catabolic pathway that is distinct from the (D)-arabinonic acid catabolic pathways that are present in many other organisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the enolase (2-phospho-D-glycerate hydro-lyase; EC 4.2.1.11) superfamily is an ancient and versatile enzyme family that has evolved to carry out a wide variety of biochemical transformations.

the E. coli genome has the genetic potential to catabolize (D)-gluconic and galactonic acid, as well as their respective uronic acids, and that the genes encoding the enzymes of the pathway are located in three transcriptional clusters.

, in addition to the well-known (L)-idaric acid pathway, E. coli has the capacity to metabolize both (D)- and (L)-hexaric acids via a pathway that generates 2-oxo-3-hydroxy-4-phosphohexanoate (OHPHA).
